content: A medical ventilator is an automated device designed to mechanically deliver breathable air into and out of the lungs. It is used to provide respiratory support for patients who are unable to breathe on their own or are breathing inadequately. Ventilators are primarily utilized in intensive care units, home care settings, emergency medicine, and as part of anesthesia machines during surgical procedures. The air reservoir is pneumatically compressed multiple times per minute to deliver either room air or a mixture of air and oxygen to the patient. Exhaled air is typically expelled through a one-way valve in the patient circuit. The oxygen concentration in the delivered gas can be adjusted from 21% (ambient air) to 100% (pure oxygen). They often include backup batteries, oxygen tanks, and remote control capabilities. These fine-tuned settings not only optimize ventilation but also enhance patient comfort and tolerance. In countries like Germany, Canada, and the United States, respiratory therapists are responsible for adjusting these settings. The patient circuit typically consists of three lightweight plastic tubes, each serving a distinct function (e.g. Depending on the type of ventilation required, the patient-end of the circuit can be either noninvasive or invasive. Noninvasive ventilation, often used for patients who only need support during sleep or rest, typically involves a nasal mask. Invasive ventilation, required for long-term dependence, usually involves a tracheostomy tube, which is more comfortable and practical for extended use compared to laryngeal or nasal intubation. Mechanical ventilators are classified as life-critical systems because their failure can result in death. They often include manual backup mechanisms for hand-driven ventilation in case of power outages. Additionally, many systems are equipped with compressed gas tanks, backup batteries, and fail-safe mechanisms to maintain functionality during power or gas supply interruptions. Some systems also feature methods to alert caregivers or summon help in the event of mechanical or software failures. The Drinker respirator, introduced in 1928, and subsequent improvements by John Haven Emerson in 1931, were pivotal in this era. In 1949, Emerson collaborated with Harvard University’s anesthesia department to develop a mechanical anesthesia assister. The 1950s saw a rise in the use of mechanical ventilators in anesthesia and intensive care, driven by the need to treat polio patients and the increasing use of muscle relaxants during surgery. These drugs, while improving surgical conditions, paralyze respiratory muscles, necessitating mechanical ventilation. In the United States, the Bird ventilator was an early gas-driven model that required no electrical power. In the United Kingdom, early examples included the East Radcliffe and Beaver models, the latter powered by an automotive wiper motor. However, electric motors posed explosion risks in operating rooms due to the presence of flammable anesthetics like ether and cyclopropane. In 1952, Roger Manley of Westminster Hospital in London developed a gas-driven ventilator that became widely popular in Europe. This design, known as the Manley ventilator, was independent of electrical power and posed no explosion hazard. The Mark I model evolved into the Manley Mark II, manufactured by the Blease company. Its operation was simple: incoming gas flow lifted a weighted bellows, which then fell under gravity to deliver breathing gases to the patient. High-frequency percussive ventilation (HFPV) emerged in the 1980s as a hybrid of conventional mechanical ventilation and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation. It has been used in specialized centers to manage patients with persistent hypoxemia unresponsive to conventional ventilation. In some cases, HFPV is employed as the primary mode of ventilatory support from the outset.
